texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction combined with an incomplete instrument cross-check, did not maintain the traffic pattern altitude published in the LAP. Altitude excursions exceeded 300 feet on downwind and continued to diverge on the base leg. The IP had to take the controls to re-establish the aircraft on pattern altitude before the aircraft became a factor to other traffic.
texts.1: SP, due to an instrument cross-check that stayed outside the cockpit while maneuvering, did not hold the pattern altitude of the LAP. Deviations reached the 300 foot limit on downwind and base and were arrested only after repeated verbal altitude calls from the IP. SP did not detect the trend on his own at any point of the circuit.
texts.2: SP, due to trim not being refined after the level-off at pattern altitude, allowed the altitude to drift while flying the pattern legs. Deviations stayed between 150 and 300 feet, SP identified them on the altimeter and returned the aircraft to pattern altitude in time and without any IP intervention. The remaining legs were flown on altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern altitude of the LAP within 150 feet throughout the circuit, on every leg and during the turns. SP trimmed the aircraft after the level-off and corrected the small deviations that appeared immediately, using precise and smooth control and power inputs. The altitude cross-check ran continuously in parallel with the lookout.
texts.4: SP flew the whole traffic pattern with altitude deviations of only a few tens of feet, well inside the required tolerance. The aircraft was trimmed correctly, the level-off at pattern altitude was accurate and altitude was preserved unchanged through the turns and the configuration changes. Corrections were anticipatory rather than reactive.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern altitude within standards, but this axis was marginal: deviations repeatedly approached 150 feet, with a consistent tendency to descend below the LAP pattern altitude during the downwind and base turns. Corrections were correct but were applied after the deviation had developed rather than at its onset. SP is expected to anticipate the altitude loss in the turns and to hold the pattern altitude with a clearly narrower margin in the following sorties.

texts.0: SP, due to power management that lagged behind the configuration changes, did not stabilize the aircraft on the airspeeds prescribed for the traffic pattern. Deviations exceeded 20 knots on downwind and grew further during the base turn, leaving the aircraft fast and displaced from the pattern. The IP had to intervene on the throttle and the controls to bring the aircraft back to the correct pattern speed.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed retrimming after each configuration change, did not hold the pattern airspeeds of the LAP. Deviations reached the 20 knot limit and were reduced only after successive verbal power and airspeed calls by the IP. SP did not connect the airspeed error to the power setting on his own initiative.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the airspeed indication after the level-off, allowed the pattern airspeed to drift. Errors stayed between 10 and 20 knots, SP identified them during the cross-check and re-established the prescribed airspeed in time and without IP intervention. The remaining legs were flown on speed.
texts.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern airspeeds within 10 knots on every leg of the circuit. Power was set early for each configuration change, the aircraft was retrimmed and the small airspeed errors were corrected immediately with smooth throttle inputs. The airspeed indication was cross-checked continuously against the aircraft attitude.
texts.4: SP flew the traffic pattern with airspeed deviations of only a few knots throughout the circuit. Power changes were anticipatory, the aircraft was stabilized on the prescribed speed for each leg without oscillation, and the airspeed was preserved unchanged through the turns and the configuration changes.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern airspeeds within standards, but this axis was marginal: errors repeatedly approached 10 knots, with a persistent tendency to remain fast after the downwind level-off. The corrections were correct but late, so the airspeed was regained close to the turn to base rather than early on the leg. SP is expected to set power earlier for each configuration change and to hold the pattern airspeed with a clearly narrower margin.

texts.0: SP, due to turns started and stopped without reference to the runway heading and the LAP pattern geometry, did not roll out on the headings required for the pattern legs. Roll-out errors exceeded 10 degrees and were not corrected, so the aircraft ended up off the published ground track and off the assigned ATC heading. The IP had to take the controls to re-establish the aircraft on the correct pattern leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll-out anticipation that was not adjusted for the bank angle used, did not stop the turns on the required leg headings. Errors reached the 10 degree limit on more than one leg and were corrected only after the IP called the heading. SP did not detect the roll-out error himself.
texts.2: SP, due to a heading cross-check interrupted by the configuration changes, rolled out off the required leg headings. Errors stayed between 5 and 10 degrees, SP recognized them on the HSI and re-established the correct heading in time and without IP intervention, keeping the pattern leg within the published track.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the required pattern leg headings within 5 degrees on every turn of the circuit. Roll-out was anticipated correctly for the bank angle used, the residual errors were corrected immediately and each leg was flown on the heading required by the LAP and by ATC.
texts.4: SP flew every turn of the traffic pattern with roll-out errors of only a couple of degrees. Turns were started at the correct points, roll-out anticipation matched the bank angle exactly and the leg headings were then held unchanged without any further correction.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out on the leg headings within standards, but this axis was marginal: errors repeatedly approached 5 degrees, consistently in the direction of overshooting the turn to the downwind. The corrections were prompt but were needed on almost every turn instead of the roll-out being accurate first time. SP is expected to refine the roll-out anticipation for the bank angle flown and to stop the turns on heading with a clearly narrower margin.

error_modes.label: Ground track over the published pattern points

texts.0: SP, due to visual pattern points identified late and a drift correction that was never applied, did not overfly the points of the traffic pattern as they are described in the LAP. The aircraft passed outside the maximum radius of 0.5 NM at more than one point and the resulting track placed it into the pattern of the adjacent leg. The IP had to intervene and re-position the aircraft on the published track.
texts.1: SP, due to the pattern points being flown from memory instead of being acquired visually, did not fly the published traffic pattern track accurately. The aircraft passed at the 0.5 NM limit at the pattern points and returned to the published track only after the IP pointed out the reference features. SP did not perceive the displacement on his own.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind drift correction applied later than the turn onto the leg, drifted off the ground track described in the LAP. Displacement remained inside the maximum radius of 0.5 NM, SP identified the reference points and re-established the aircraft on the published track in time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP overflew all the points of the traffic pattern as they are described in the LAP, comfortably inside the maximum radius of 0.5 NM. Each point was acquired visually in time, the drift correction was applied on the leg from the beginning and the pattern was flown with a stable and repeatable ground track.
texts.4: SP flew the traffic pattern essentially over the published points, with displacement that was negligible against the maximum radius of 0.5 NM. Visual references were acquired well in advance, wind drift was anticipated on each leg and the resulting track was identical to the pattern described in the LAP.
texts.marginal: SP overflew the pattern points inside the 0.5 NM radius required by the LAP, but this axis was marginal: the aircraft repeatedly passed near the outer edge of the permitted radius, consistently wide on the downwind leg with a crosswind from the runway side. The reference points were acquired correctly but late, so the drift correction was applied after the displacement had built up. SP is expected to anticipate the drift on each leg and to overfly the published points with a clearly tighter track.

error_modes.label: Spacing from other pattern traffic and clearing

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that stayed inside the cockpit and the absence of active monitoring of the preceding aircraft, did not maintain proper spacing to the other traffic in the pattern and did not clear constantly. The preceding aircraft was allowed to close to a distance that made the sequence unworkable and the conflict was not recognized by SP at any stage. The IP had to intervene and direct an extension of the leg to restore separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout limited to the direction of flight, did not maintain proper spacing to the traffic ahead in the pattern and cleared only intermittently. Spacing eroded to the point where the IP had to call the traffic, and SP extended the leg only after that call. The recovery was correct but entirely prompted.
texts.2: SP, due to a lookout that was interrupted during the configuration changes, allowed the spacing to the preceding aircraft to reduce below what the sequence required. SP re-established the constant clearing scan, identified the closure himself and adjusted the leg in time to restore proper spacing, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained proper spacing to all other traffic in the pattern while clearing constantly. The preceding and following aircraft were monitored visually and by radio throughout the circuit, and the pattern legs were adjusted early and smoothly so that the sequence was maintained without any prompting.
texts.4: SP kept the clearing scan running continuously through every leg and turn of the pattern and maintained accurate spacing to all other traffic without any prompting. Adjustments to the legs were anticipatory, based on the position of the preceding aircraft, and the sequence was preserved with no rushed corrections at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained proper spacing and cleared throughout the pattern within standards, but this axis was marginal: the clearing scan lapsed each time attention shifted to the configuration changes, and spacing to the aircraft ahead was allowed to reduce more than the sequence needed before being adjusted. The corrections were effective but reactive. SP is expected to keep the clearing scan uninterrupted during checks and configuration changes and to adjust the legs earlier from the position of the preceding aircraft.

texts.0: SP, due to standard phraseology not being used and the transmissions being composed in the air, did not give all the standardized position reports. Mandatory reports for the pattern were omitted, ATC had to query the aircraft position and the IP had to make the calls himself so that the sequence would remain clear to the other traffic.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology and reports assembled while flying instead of being prepared before the point, did not give the standardized position reports at the required points. Each report was transmitted only after the IP prompted it, and the wording had to be corrected before the call was intelligible to the other traffic.
texts.2: SP, due to a report initiated in non-standard wording, transmitted one pattern position report late and imprecisely. SP recognized the departure from standard phraseology himself, corrected the transmission on his own initiative and gave all the remaining reports at the required points and in standard form, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP gave all the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern at the required points and in the standard phraseology. The transmissions were short, correctly worded and made without disturbing the flying of the leg, so the position of the aircraft in the sequence was clear to ATC and to the other traffic at all times.
texts.4: SP transmitted every standardized pattern position report exactly at the required point, in faultless standard phraseology and with no repetition or correction needed. Each call was prepared before the point was reached, and the radio work never competed with the flying of the pattern.
texts.marginal: SP gave the standardized position reports within standards, but this axis was marginal: several calls were made slightly after the reporting point and the phraseology drifted toward informal wording under the workload of the base turn. The reports were complete and intelligible, but they were composed in the air rather than prepared in advance. SP is expected to prepare each call before reaching the reporting point and to keep to standard phraseology throughout the circuit.

error_modes.label: Radio monitoring and traffic picture against ATC instructions

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of the traffic picture while the attention was captured by the pattern flying, did not monitor the radio and did not check the position of the other aircraft according to their position reports and the ATC instructions. Instructions addressed to the aircraft were missed, the readback was wrong and SP had no awareness of where the other traffic was in the pattern. The IP had to take over the radio and direct the aircraft back into the sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental picture of the pattern that was never updated from the transmissions of the other aircraft, did not check the position of the other traffic against their position reports and the ATC instructions. Calls addressed to the aircraft had to be repeated by ATC and relayed by the IP before SP responded and complied. SP did not rebuild the traffic picture on his own.
texts.2: SP, due to attention drawn to a configuration change at the moment of a transmission, missed one ATC call and lost part of the traffic picture. SP identified the gap himself, requested a repeat, re-established the position of the other traffic from their subsequent reports and complied with the instruction in time, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP monitored the radio continuously and checked the position of the other aircraft according to their position reports and the ATC instructions throughout the pattern. All instructions were received, read back correctly and complied with, and the position of the other traffic was known at every stage of the circuit.
texts.4: SP maintained a complete and current picture of the pattern traffic from the radio at all times, correlating every position report with the visual acquisition of the aircraft concerned. ATC instructions were anticipated, read back faultlessly and executed without any degradation of the flying, and the traffic picture was never interrupted.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the radio and kept track of the other traffic within standards, but this axis was marginal: the traffic picture went stale during the workload peaks of the pattern and had to be rebuilt from later transmissions rather than being maintained continuously. All instructions were eventually received and complied with, but two readbacks were delayed. SP is expected to keep updating the position of the other aircraft from their reports throughout the circuit, including during configuration changes.

error_modes.label: Descent planning and arrival at the entry point

texts.0: SP, due to a descent started late and pre-descent procedures and checks left incomplete, did not achieve the assigned altitude before the entry point. The aircraft arrived at the authorized VFR entry point more than 300 feet off the assigned altitude and still in the descent, with the checks unfinished and the entry procedure not established. The IP had to take the controls and manage the descent and the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent profile not computed against the distance remaining to the entry point, did not carry out the pre-descent procedures and checks in time. The aircraft reached the assigned altitude at the 300 foot limit right at the entry point, and only after the IP called for the descent and for the outstanding checks. SP did not recognize the profile error himself.
texts.2: SP, due to a top-of-descent point selected without allowing for the tailwind, began the descent from the assigned area later than planned. The deviation from the assigned altitude at the entry point remained between 150 and 300 feet, SP identified the profile error in time, completed the pre-descent procedures and checks and established the assigned altitude before entering the pattern, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP departed the assigned flight area as determined in the LAP and according to the ATC instructions, carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks in time and achieved the assigned altitude before the authorized VFR entry point. The entry into the traffic pattern was made from the standard entry point, following the ATC directives without any misapprehension.
texts.4: SP planned the return and descent so that the aircraft was level on the assigned altitude, fully configured and with all pre-descent checks complete well before the entry point. The departure from the area, the descent and the entry from the standard point ran exactly to the ATC directives, with the entry procedure and the following points anticipated throughout.
texts.marginal: SP achieved the assigned altitude before the entry point and completed the pre-descent procedures within standards, but this axis was marginal: the descent was started late enough that the checks and the level-off were compressed into the last part of the leg, and the aircraft steadied on altitude only shortly before the entry point. SP is expected to compute the top-of-descent point against the distance remaining and to complete the pre-descent procedures and checks with a clear margin before the entry point.

error_modes.label: Formation positioning for BREAK and direction to the active runway

texts.0: SP, on the formation sortie, did not place the wingman to the right position for BREAK execution and did not direct the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY, due to the active runway and the break direction not being confirmed before the entry. The formation arrived at the break point with the wingman on the wrong side and the landing pattern procedures described in the LAP could not be followed. The IP had to intervene, take over the lead of the formation and re-establish it for the break.
texts.1: SP, on the formation sortie, did not position the wingman correctly for BREAK execution, due to a crossunder called too late in the run-in. The formation reached the BREAK of the active RWY at the limit of a workable geometry and only after the IP directed the repositioning and the timing of the calls. SP did not identify the incorrect side himself.
texts.2: SP, on the formation sortie, initially set up the formation for a break on the wrong side of the active RWY, due to the wind check being read after the entry point rather than before it. SP identified the error, called the crossunder and placed the wingman to the correct position for BREAK execution in time, directing the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY and following the landing pattern procedures of the LAP without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP placed the wingman to the right position for BREAK execution and directed the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY correctly. The active runway and the break direction were confirmed before the entry point, the repositioning was called in time and the formation followed the landing pattern procedures as described in the LAP.
texts.4: SP led the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY with the wingman placed in exactly the right position and the repositioning completed well before the run-in. The break direction was established from the wind and the ATC directives early, the calls were clear and timely, and the landing pattern procedures of the LAP were followed precisely by the whole formation.
texts.marginal: SP placed the wingman for BREAK execution and directed the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY within standards, but this axis was marginal: the break direction was confirmed close to the entry point and the crossunder was called late enough that the wingman was steady in position only shortly before the run-in. The result was correct but compressed. SP is expected to confirm the active runway and break direction earlier and to complete the wingman repositioning with a clear margin before the break.

error_modes.label: Use of navigation aids for orientation in the airport environment

texts.0: SP, due to the VOR/DME, TACAN and GPS not being set up during the return, did not use them to become orientated with the airport environment when this was required. With the visual references degraded, SP could not establish the position relative to the authorized VFR entry points and continued toward the airport without a usable position reference. The IP had to provide the position and direct the aircraft to the entry point.
texts.1: SP, due to navigation aids tuned but never identified or cross-checked, did not use them for the return and the orientation with the airport environment. The position relative to the entry points was established at the limit of a workable margin and only after the IP directed the selection and interpretation of the aid. SP did not use the available equipment on his own initiative.
texts.2: SP, due to the navigation aid being selected later than the departure from the assigned area, was slow to become orientated with the airport environment. SP identified the omission, tuned and identified the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS, established the position relative to the authorized entry points in time and completed the return to the entry point without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP used the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS where it was required in order to be orientated with the airport environment and used them for the return. The aids were tuned and identified in time, the indications were cross-checked against the visual references and the position relative to the authorized VFR entry points was known throughout the return.
texts.4: SP set up and identified the navigation aids before departing the assigned area and used them continuously to cross-check the visual picture during the return. The position relative to the airport environment and the authorized VFR entry points was established at all times without any doubt, and the aids were interpreted correctly and without any additional workload.
texts.marginal: SP used the navigation aids for the return and the orientation with the airport environment within standards, but this axis was marginal: the aids were tuned and identified only after the departure from the assigned area, and the indications were consulted rather than cross-checked continuously against the visual references. The orientation was correct but was rebuilt each time it was needed. SP is expected to set up and identify the aids before leaving the area and to keep the position relative to the entry points continuously cross-checked.
